title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Inside the Machine: How KORU Manufactures 300% Daily Korea Exposure

epigraph.quote: An index fund owns the market; a leveraged ETF rents the market's daily variance from prime broker balance sheets.
epigraph.author: Institutional Derivatives Desk Axiom

web_blocks.html: Unlike an operating conglomerate, KORU does not run manufacturing plants or software subscriptions [1]. Instead, it generates economic exposure through a three-pillar portfolio architecture disclosed in its audited Form N-CSR Schedule of Investments [1]. The fund targets 300% of the daily return of the MSCI Korea 25/50 Index [1][2][6]. To achieve this goal, Rafferty Asset Management does not purchase local Won-denominated shares on the Korea Exchange [1]. Doing so would create overnight settlement bottlenecks for NYSE Arca creation and redemption activity [1]. Instead, the manager combines U.S.-listed index ETF shares, institutional money market collateral, and over-the-counter (OTC) total return swap contracts [1].

web_blocks.explanatory_p: At October 31, 2025, KORU held $122.51M in physical EWY shares alongside $461.65M in swap notional and $132.46M in unrealized swap appreciation [1]. Segregated collateral stood against $240.60M in fund net assets [1]. Together, these sleeves delivered ~298% effective daily exposure to the MSCI Korea 25/50 benchmark [1].
web_blocks.takeaway: KORU is a hybrid physical-plus-swap engine: 50.9% physical EWY, 44.6% Treasury/government money market collateral earning ~4% yield, and ~192% base notional in OTC swaps across four Tier-1 banks [1].

web_blocks.html: On the underlying equity side, KORU's economic exposure mirrors the MSCI Korea 25/50 Index [2][4]. South Korea's stock market is heavily concentrated in memory semiconductors [4]. In standard uncapped Korean indices, Samsung Electronics routinely exceeds 30% of total market capitalization [4]. To comply with U.S. Regulated Investment Company (RIC) tax rules, MSCI applies a 25/50 capping methodology [4]. MSCI recalibrates this rule at quarterly rebalances in February, May, August, and November [4]. Under this framework, no single issuer may exceed 25% of the index [4]. the aggregate weight of all issuers above 5% cannot exceed 50% [4]. Even with these regulatory caps, the benchmark remains a concentrated wager on global technology hardware and Korean industrial champions [4].

A concrete example illustrates what a $10,000 allocation to KORU actually owns on a look-through basis [1][4]. At 3x daily leverage, that allocation commands $30,000 of gross Korean equity beta [1][4]. Roughly $12,600 to $14,400 of that exposure (42%–48% of the index) sits in just two memory-semiconductor titans [4]. These are Samsung Electronics (~22%–23% weight) and SK Hynix (~19%–24% weight) [4]. Their corporate earnings track global AI data-center HBM3e and HBM4 demand, server DRAM pricing, and smartphone cycles [4]. Another major allocation block sits in leading Korean financials, including KB Financial Group, Shinhan Financial, and Hana Financial [4]. It also holds major automotive and industrial exporters like Hyundai Motor and Kia [4]. These cyclical leaders represent the primary beneficiaries of Seoul's Corporate Value-Up Program [4]. That state initiative seeks to lift corporate dividends, expand share buybacks, and boost depressed price-to-book valuations [4].

web_blocks.title: Why EWY Swaps Instead of Direct KOSPI Futures?
paragraphs: In the FY2025 Schedule of Investments, every OTC swap contract references the total return of the iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY) rather than local KOSPI 200 futures [1]. Using EWY as the reference asset aligns KORU's 4:00 PM ET net asset value strike with U.S. market hours [1]. This structure eliminates overnight Korean Won and exchange settlement friction for Authorized Participants [1]. It also enables swap dealers to hedge their exposures cleanly using deep U.S. equity liquidity [1].

web_blocks.html: In a 1940 Act ETF, fund-level 'revenue' consists of Investment Income [1]. This income includes cash dividends received on physical EWY shares and interest earned on Treasury and money market collateral [1]. In FY2025, KORU generated $3,807,379 in total investment income [1]. Of that sum, $2,215,892 (58.2%) came from interest on Dreyfus and Goldman Sachs government money market funds [1]. Those collateral funds yielded 3.89%–4.05% as of October 31, 2025 [1]. The remaining $1,591,487 (41.8%) arrived through dividend distributions on physical EWY shares [1]. Short-term U.S. Treasury interest rates play a central role in KORU's internal cash economics [1]. When T-bill yields sit near 4%, the fund's 44.6% cash-collateral sleeve generates substantial yield [1]. This interest income helps offset both the 0.75% advisory fee and SOFR-linked swap financing charges [1].

The MSCI 25/50 capping rule directly alters KORU's sector mix during semiconductor booms [4]. In an uncapped Korean market-cap benchmark, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix together can exceed 50% of total index weight [4]. MSCI's optimization algorithm forces all constituents larger than 5% to sum to no more than 50% in aggregate [4]. Therefore, any excess weight above the threshold is redistributed to the next tier of Korean blue chips [4]. Beneficiaries include commercial banks like KB Financial and Shinhan Financial [4]. They also include automakers like Hyundai Motor and Kia, alongside tech holdings like Naver and SK Square [4]. In this manner, KORU provides a regulated portfolio blend [4]. It delivers roughly half memory-semiconductor beta and half cyclical Value-Up financials and industrials [4].

book_paragraphs: If you crack open the hood of KORU, you will not find a single Korean won sitting in a Seoul brokerage account, nor will you find shares of Samsung Electronics or Hyundai Motor held directly in the fund's custody vault. Instead, as the October 31, 2025 audited Schedule of Investments in Direxion's Form N-CSR reveals, KORU is an ingenious three-part financial assembly built entirely inside U.S. dollar plumbing.

The first pillar is a physical equity sleeve. At the end of fiscal year 2025, KORU held 1,263,033 shares of the iShares MSCI South Korea ETF—ticker EWY—valued at $122.51 million, or 50.9% of the fund's $240.60 million in net assets. Why hold EWY instead of buying Korean stocks directly? Because EWY trades in New York during the exact same 9:30 AM to 4:00 PM Eastern window as KORU, settles in U.S. dollars, and already handles the complex foreign-exchange conversions and Korean custody rules. Holding half the fund in EWY also gives KORU real dividend income—$1.59 million in FY2025—and serves as high-grade collateral.

The second pillar is a cash and Treasury collateral sleeve totaling $107.28 million, or 44.6% of net assets, parked across institutional money market funds from Dreyfus and Goldman Sachs yielding between 3.89% and 4.05%. Together with part of the EWY stake, $150.05 million of KORU's assets were formally segregated as collateral to back its derivative book. And that collateral is not idle: in FY2025, it produced $2.22 million in interest income, accounting for 58.2% of the fund's $3.81 million total investment income.

The third pillar is where the 3x leverage actually lives: four over-the-counter total return swap agreements with Tier-1 global investment banks. On October 31, 2025, KORU's swap book comprised $77.94 million notional with Bank of America Merrill Lynch at SOFR plus 60 basis points, $89.08 million with Citibank at SOFR plus 85 basis points, $83.51 million with Barclays at SOFR plus 70 basis points, and $211.12 million with J.P. Morgan at SOFR plus 70 basis points. Combined with $132.46 million in unrealized swap appreciation and the $122.51 million physical EWY stake, those contracts gave KORU roughly 298% effective daily exposure to South Korean equities.

Now translate that structure into concrete economic reality. When you hold $10,000 of KORU for a single day, you are controlling $30,000 of look-through exposure to the MSCI Korea 25/50 Index. Even though MSCI's 25/50 rule caps any single issuer at 25% and all issuers above 5% at 50% combined, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix together still command roughly 42% to 48% of the index. That means nearly half of your $30,000 notional bet is riding on two Korean memory-chip makers—and by extension on global AI server spending, High-Bandwidth Memory yields, and DRAM pricing—while the rest is spread across Korean banks, automakers like Hyundai Motor, and industrial exporters caught up in Seoul's Value-Up governance push.

Notice one subtle twist that most traders miss when they compare KORU to the domestic KOSPI index in Seoul. In an uncapped Korean benchmark, a runaway rally in either Samsung Electronics or SK Hynix can push their combined weight past 50%. Under MSCI's 25/50 methodology, every quarterly rebalance in February, May, August, and November mechanically trims those two giants back under the 25% single-issuer and 50% aggregate ceilings, redistributing the excess weight down into Korean financials like KB Financial and industrials like Hyundai Motor. That means KORU is structurally slightly more diversified than an uncapped KOSPI bet during a single-stock semiconductor mania, while still remaining overwhelmingly levered to Korea's export and memory cycle.

Equally important is the mark-to-market mechanics of the swap book itself. Look back at that $132.46 million of unrealized appreciation sitting on KORU's swap contracts on October 31, 2025. As the underlying EWY shares rallied during FY2025, the swaps accumulated huge positive mark-to-market gains before their scheduled December 2025 and November 2026 termination dates. At each reset or termination, those gains are settled in cash between KORU and its four dealer banks—which is why KORU's Statement of Assets and Liabilities also showed $121.80 million due to brokers for swap collateral and reset adjustments. You are not just looking at a static ETF; you are looking at a living, breathing daily collateral-and-margin clearinghouse.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Understanding that KORU is 50.9% EWY, 44.6% T-bill money markets, and 192% OTC swaps changes how you think about its costs. You are not just paying an expense ratio to Direxion; you are paying SOFR plus 60 to 85 basis points to four Wall Street banks for synthetic leverage, partially offset by the T-bill yield earned on your cash collateral and the dividends paid by EWY.

section_takeaway: KORU manufactures 300% daily MSCI Korea 25/50 exposure by pairing physical EWY shares (50.9%) and Treasury/government money market collateral (44.6%) with OTC total return swaps across four Tier-1 banks priced at SOFR + 60–85 bps [1].
